extracted.intended_audience: school teachers (especially beginners in common/country schools)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for arranging schoolrooms, managing pupil behavior, and organising teaching so the teacher can attend to one thing at a time while pupils remain steadily employed. Emphasizes planning, observation, and moral/intellectual methods over coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer moral and intellectual means over coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not endeavor to drive them as a man drives a herd, by mere peremptory command or half angry blows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the nature of the effect to be produced and of the materials upon which you are to work, adopt a plan founded upon principles which ought to regulate the action of mind upon mind, and adapted to produce the intellectual effect desired. Avoid scolding, ridicule, or corporal/harsh punishment as primary tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher must be intellectually interested in experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A teacher, while trying new measures, must have been interested in his intellectual experiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After forming a plan, the teacher should watch with strong interest its operation (walk round the room, observe effects), not interrupt the exercise, and use observed results to refine future plans. Interest helps avoid dull routine and turns practice into inquiry about cause and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use emulation and rewards targeted at effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Appeal to emulation: offer prizes not for 'best' but for most appearance of 'effort' and 'care' for a period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer incentives (e.g., pencils) as rewards for demonstrated effort rather than absolute excellence. Observe who makes effort; do not necessarily single out praise initially—use prizes to stimulate emulation and engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make rewards accessible to the majority
rubrics_metrics.description: One or two prizes will not influence the majority; multiply prizes to bring one within reach of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divide prizes (e.g., split two pencils into quarters to create eight prizes) so each small group has a realistic chance; recognize that the 'honor of the victory' is the real prize and that perceived attainability increases participation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe interventions without interrupting regular work
rubrics_metrics.description: While performing these experiments and watching results, pupils should go on undisturbed in their pursuits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not interrupt exercises to test measures. Walk round, note who changes behavior, and let exercises continue to avoid deranging the steady acquisition of knowledge. Variations in method must not destroy uniform progress toward permanent objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confine variations to modes of accomplishing permanent objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be variety in methods and plan; through all this variety, the school... must go steadily forward in the acquisition of that knowledge which is of greatest importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any inventive or varied method must be aimed at the same permanent educational objectives and should not disrupt the core learning process. Save experimental creativity for modes, not for changing the fundamental aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate and be prepared for pupil offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Some teachers seem never to make it a part of their calculation that their pupils will do wrong; others expect them and are prepared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think ahead about the typical misconducts and dullness of children; be prepared to handle ordinary infractions calmly rather than being surprised and irritated when they occur. Preparation does not mean indifference, but readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your materials 'just as they are'
rubrics_metrics.description: Make yourself acquainted with these materials, just as they are.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurately assess pupils' capacities and tendencies before designing plans. Avoid expecting from them what is not reasonable; adapt measures to realistic capabilities to prevent chronic frustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Count the cost; understand real difficulties beforehand
rubrics_metrics.description: It is best, if there are any real and peculiar sources of trial and difficulty in this pursuit, that they should be distinctly known and acknowledged at the outset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be honest about the burdens of teaching (moral responsibility, multiplicity of particulars). Overrate rather than underrate the challenges so you can plan accordingly and avoid surprise and discouragement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept moral responsibility as part of the role
rubrics_metrics.description: The first great difficulty ... is a sort of moral responsibility for the conduct of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that teachers commonly feel responsible for pupils' misconduct and that this is a unique and heavy burden; acknowledge it so you can manage its emotional effects on your health and work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematize and classify to reduce multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: He must be systematic. He must classify and arrange; but after he has done all that he can, he must still expect that his daily business will continue to consist of a vast multitude of minute particulars.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classification and system to reduce bewildering particulars. Arrange work so the teacher can attend to one thing at a time rather than trying to do many simultaneous tasks; plan the day's work to avoid constant multi-tasking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim general arrangements at two objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects then, to be aimed at in the general arrangements of schools, are two-fold: (1) That the teacher may be left uninterrupted, to attend to one thing at a time. (2) That the individual scholars may have constant employment, and such an amount and such kinds of study, as shall be suited to the circumstances and capacities of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design schedules, grouping, and routines so the teacher gets focused time and pupils have continuous, appropriately leveled work. Balance teacher attention and pupil activity through organizational measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and remove constant sources of interruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The principal things which ... press upon the teacher: (1) Giving leave to whisper or to leave seats. (2) Mending pens. (3) Answering questions in regard to studies. (4) Hearing recitations. (5) Watching the behavior of the scholars. (6) Administering reproof and punishment for offences as they occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list and address recurring interruptions via rules, scheduling, routines, or delegation so they do not demand constant simultaneous attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate whispering and leaving seats by set 'study hours'
rubrics_metrics.description: Appropriate particular times at which all this business is to be done, and forbid it altogether at every other time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give short general permission periods (e.g., two or three minutes every hour or every half hour) for whispering/seat changes instead of individual requests. Use a visible 'STUDY HOURS' card, a bell to mark times, and train pupils to wait until the card is taken down.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure pupil cooperation and a majority in support of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: It is of fundamental importance that the pupils should themselves be interested in it. Their cooperation, or rather the cooperation of the majority, which it is very easy to obtain, is absolutely essential to success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present changes as common-interest arrangements, involve pupils in decisions (e.g., frequency of rests), solicit voluntary participation, and aim to mobilize a large majority so a small minority can be managed without disrupting the plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train pupils to self-monitor via voluntary reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: I wish every one would keep an exact account ... of all the instances of speaking and leaving seats, and be prepared to report them at the close of the school.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use daily self-report exercises (calls for standing and reporting counts/categories of transgressions) without punishment initially to accustom pupils to honest reporting; start with small, pleasant-group reporting and iterate to establish habit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make enforcement pleasant and experimental, not punitive
rubrics_metrics.description: All however, should be done in a pleasant tone, and with a pleasant and cheerful air. It should be considered by the pupils, not a reluctant confession of guilt, for which they are to be rebuked or punished, but the voluntary and free report of the result of an experiment, in which all are interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame accountability as collective experiment and improvement rather than shaming. Praise voluntary cooperation and avoid making reporting feel like confession; use good-humored assistance to train adherence rather than threats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw precise lines and require small inconveniences for common good
rubrics_metrics.description: We must, therefore, draw a precise line, and individuals must submit to a little inconvenience, sometimes, to promote the general good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow ad hoc exceptions that will erode rules (e.g., letting one pupil frequently leave for minor reasons). Set clear boundaries and expect occasional small inconveniences in service of the rule's durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect an adjustment period and train, don't punish, initially
rubrics_metrics.description: You cannot reasonably expect ... it will, at once, go into full and complete operation. They must be trained, not by threatening and punishment, but by your good-humored assistance, to their new duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate lapses during the first days; use reminders, light coaching, and self-reporting to build habit rather than immediate punishment. Allow measured time for the new order to become established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ignore petty opposition from a small minority
rubrics_metrics.description: Among such, there would generally be some, who would refuse to have any thing to do with the measure, just from a desire to thwart and impede the plans of the teacher. If so, it is best to take no notice of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a majority supports a change, do not let a few dissenters derail it; focus on maintaining majority practice and let opposition fade by non-recognition rather than amplifying it.
